title: About Cognitive Overload - 1
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Martin Skelton begins a two-part treatment of cognitive overload, which he presents, following Dylan Wiliam, as arguably the single most important thing for teachers to know. He grounds it in the brain's heavy energy use and its habit of conserving energy through hardwired repetition, so that overload is what happens when the brain's energy is already spent before a task begins. He distinguishes it carefully from distraction, using examples from interrogation, meditation and road rage. Drawing on Hattie and Yates, he explains the limits of working memory and how long-term schemas let an expert treat a big picture as one item, using his own expertise versus his kitchen-cupboard helplessness as illustrations. He concludes that overload has no learning benefit and flags a follow-up on how it shows up for students, teachers, leaders and parents.
points: Cognitive overload is framed as an energy problem: the brain has already used up its supply before the task starts, so even simple material cannot be processed.
Skelton separates overload from distraction, since a distracted person can recover with self-discipline while an overloaded one lacks the energy to do so.
Working memory holds only a few items for seconds, but long-term schemas let experts treat a whole big picture as a single item, which explains why newcomers struggle more.
Everyday cases such as a heated argument before writing, interrogation and road rage show overload is common and not confined to classrooms.
Because good struggle itself costs brain energy, he argues that ignoring overload only harms learning.
quotes: Cognitive overload has been described by Dylan William, one of the UK’s leading researchers in, and synthesisers about, learning, as ‘the single most important thing for teachers to know.’ It’s a big claim but it is an important one. Dylan William is someone not prone to making outrageous statements about his work.

Distraction is a failure to hold my focus. It can be caused by loud music from the next room, the dog barking, an email subject that flashes on my screen and looks more interesting than I should allow it to and so on. With distractions I can, with a little self-discipline, get myself back on track.

Cognitive Overload is not a distraction. It’s an inability to process sometimes simple but often complex material because the brain no longer has the energy to do so. We have already emptied our brains’ energy supply before coming to the task in hand.

There simply isn’t enough brain energy around to process how to either ignore this relatively minor incident or how to express displeasure with no more than a blast on the car horn. Instead, and before anyone knows it, two people are squaring up to each other.

What is fascinating is that these behaviours only apply to working memory. Our long-term memory - when what we have learned has been laid down as ‘sticky’ - alters what happens. Long-term memory creates ‘big pictures’ or schemas which help reduce the load on working memory, largely because the brain sees the coherent big picture in your long-term memory as one bit to work on and not the hundreds and hundreds of things the big picture actually contains.

Your working memory becomes overwhelmed when dealing with novel or disorganised information. The essential organisation to your knowledge stems from how it is stored in your long-term memory. When organisation is lacking, the mind struggles since the goal is to maintain organisation and reduce load.

There are no learning benefits to cognitive overload. It is entirely unhelpful to the process of living and to learning and getting better. The relentless daily life of schools requires significant brain energy.
